narrative:
Your application was denied because the model predicts a 52.7% chance you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. While that is not an overwhelming majority, it means the risk of failure is slightly higher than the chance of success, and the university only accepts applicants whose risk falls clearly below that line.

Three factors drove this decision, ranked by strength of influence. The most influential was your class standing in your third year. Your placement in the second decile means you finished in the bottom twenty percent of your law school class that year. Students admitted to this program typically sit around the sixth decile, so this was a significant red flag suggesting your performance slipped substantially relative to your peers.

Your undergraduate GPA was the second most important factor, and it worked in your favor. At 3.30, you exceeded the average of 3.23 for accepted students, showing you do have strong academic potential. This pulled the prediction toward passing, but not enough to overcome your law school record.

The third most influential factor was your first-year class standing. Finishing in the third decile placed you well below the typical accepted applicant's sixth-decile average. Because both your first and third year rankings were weak, the model saw a consistent pattern of struggling within a competitive law school environment.

To improve your chances, focus on raising your law school class performance, not just your raw GPA. Seek academic support, tutoring, or early bar-exam preparation to demonstrate you can master legal material. Retaking the LSAT will not address this concern; building a stronger law school record will.
